task.goal: Help new members of a research lab ask for help early without flooding a single senior researcher.
hard_constraints: Five new and three senior members; each senior has at most 20 minutes weekly for this process.
No public display of individual mistakes or mandatory personal disclosures.
Assess time to useful help, repeated blockers and senior load.
task.available_resources: Existing private chat and weekly lab meeting.
task.expected_result: A sustainable help-seeking mechanism and pilot.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Peer-first private help relay
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is to resolve routine blockers among newcomers before distributing unresolved questions across seniors. Each week, the five newcomers form a private help ring: each person has one designated first contact, with assignments rotating weekly. Members are encouraged to ask after roughly 20 minutes without progress; participation and sharing technical details remain voluntary. The first contact spends at most ten minutes helping or clarifying the question, then offers escalation rather than repeated unsuccessful troubleshooting.

Escalations go privately to one of three seniors using a rotating assignment order. Each senior has two eight-minute response slots and four minutes for reading and minimal tracking, capped at 20 minutes weekly. Questions exceeding a slot receive a bounded next step or an explicit notice that substantive help is still pending. Overflow receives the next available slot rather than silently accumulating with one senior.

This could work because newcomers often know enough to resolve setup problems or formulate clearer questions, reducing senior effort. It assumes some overlapping knowledge and willingness to help peers. It may fail when everyone lacks the same expertise, peer advice is unreliable, or newcomers feel obliged to disclose difficulties. Members may bypass the peer step for sensitive questions through the same distributed senior allocation.

Implementation needs only existing private chat, a weekly assignment message, and private request timestamps. A short lab-meeting reminder can normalize early questions without discussing individual cases. Track blocker categories only with permission; report aggregate counts without identifiable examples.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run one baseline week using current help-seeking practices, followed by a three-week relay pilot. Requesters privately record request time, first actionable response, whether it enabled progress, and recurrence of the same blocker. Seniors record all process minutes. Compare time to useful help, repeated blockers per request, and maximum individual senior load. The mechanism is challenged if the peer step consistently delays useful help, recurring blockers increase, or any senior exceeds 20 minutes. Interpret small-sample differences cautiously.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Guaranteed private micro-consultations
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is predictable access: every newcomer has a reserved private consultation, removing the need to decide whether a question deserves interrupting someone. Allocate five eight-minute appointments across the three seniors each week in a rotating 2–2–1 pattern. Each senior reserves four additional minutes for preparation and tracking, keeping the busiest allocation within 20 minutes. Unused appointments can be released to another newcomer, but total senior time cannot expand.

A newcomer may send a short question privately before the appointment or arrive without preparation. The consultation focuses on one useful next action, such as identifying the right method, narrowing an error, or choosing whom to consult. Nobody must report mistakes, explain personal circumstances, or attend if they do not need help. The lab meeting carries only scheduling information and aggregate process observations.

This could work because guaranteed access lowers the social cost of asking and spreads responsibility across seniors. Unlike a queue, it protects access for quieter members even when others ask frequently. Prerequisites are predictable availability and enough senior overlap to provide useful initial direction. Match appointments to expertise where possible while maintaining the time cap and rotating heavier assignments.

Its main limits are delay until the appointment, unused capacity, and questions too complex for eight minutes. Members can privately submit questions as soon as blocked, but the pilot must not promise immediate answers. An unresolved consultation counts as pending help, even if an appointment occurred. Existing private chat supports asynchronous eight-minute exchanges if a live conversation is impractical.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one week of current practice with three weeks of reserved access. Measure both blocker-to-request and request-to-useful-help time, repeated blockers, appointment use, and each senior’s full time commitment. Use optional private feedback to inspect whether guaranteed access made asking easier. The mechanism is challenged if appointments mainly add waiting, frequently go unused while requests remain pending, or produce conversations without actionable progress. A small pilot can reveal scheduling failures but cannot establish a reliable causal effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Senior-initiated private unblock invitations
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is proactive invitation: seniors initiate a small, predictable opportunity to ask, so newcomers do not carry the entire burden of recognizing and announcing a blocker. Assign each newcomer a rotating senior contact, distributing five people in a 2–2–1 pattern. Once weekly, each senior sends their assigned newcomers a private invitation: ‘Would a brief unblock exchange help this week? No reply is needed.’ A member can reply immediately, later, or decline without explanation.

Each senior budgets two minutes for invitations and tracking, then at most 18 minutes for responses across their assigned members. Where two members request help, each initially receives up to nine minutes. Stop at the cap and explicitly identify unresolved requests; do not treat an invitation or acknowledgement as useful help. Rotation distributes exposure to different expertise and avoids creating one permanent senior bottleneck. Members may ask between invitations, with those requests using the same weekly budget.

This could work when hesitation, uncertainty about senior availability, or fear of interrupting prevents early questions. The invitation supplies permission without requiring public reporting or personal disclosure. It requires seniors to send invitations consistently and newcomers to trust that silence has no consequences. It will be less effective if the real barrier is insufficient expertise or if members interpret invitations as performance monitoring.

Implementation uses existing private chat and a brief scheduling reminder at the weekly meeting. State explicitly that participation does not enter performance evaluation. Collect only voluntary technical blocker categories and aggregate process measures; keep individual exchanges private. This approach offers predictable outreach, but cannot guarantee enough capacity for every substantive problem.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use a four-week crossover: one balanced group of newcomers receives invitations for two weeks while the other retains self-initiated access; then switch. Both groups retain access to help within each senior’s shared 20-minute cap. Privately collect request and useful-help timestamps, optional blocker-onset estimates, repeated blockers, and senior minutes. Inspect whether invitations shorten delay before asking without worsening response time or concentrating load. The mechanism is challenged if invitations generate little additional useful help, feel coercive in optional feedback, or exhaust capacity. With five newcomers, treat comparisons as diagnostic rather than conclusive.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Private help desk with reusable answer cards
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The main mechanism is to make each useful senior answer available for reuse, reducing the senior effort required when several newcomers encounter the same obstacle. A small, searchable collection of technical answer cards lives in the existing private chat. Cards describe a task, a suggested next step, and when that advice does not apply; they contain no names, personal circumstances, or accounts of individual mistakes.

Newcomers are encouraged to ask as soon as uncertainty prevents a sensible next action. Searching the cards is optional and never a prerequisite for asking. A request goes privately to one assigned senior, with the five newcomers distributed 2–2–1 across the three seniors. Assignments provide routing; the reusable answers are what should change capacity. Seniors may reply with an existing card, adapt one, or provide fresh guidance. Requesters privately confirm whether the advice enabled progress; receiving a link alone does not count as useful help.

Each senior has a hard weekly budget of 20 minutes: up to 14 minutes for reading and answering requests, four for creating or correcting cards, and two for tracking. Once that budget is exhausted, pending requests receive a clear availability notice within the budget and remain recorded as unresolved. Card creation can be skipped when responses need the time. Only generic technical guidance is shared, with requester permission when derived from an exchange. The weekly lab meeting provides a brief reminder that early questions are welcome, without discussing individual cases.

This assumes recurring technical questions, sufficiently searchable chat, and advice that transfers between projects. It may fail for novel research problems, stale guidance, or answers that require substantial context. Start with a few common procedures already known to seniors; do not spend the pilot building a comprehensive manual.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Run one week with the same private routing and time caps but ordinary answers, then three weeks with reusable cards. Voluntarily collect request-to-confirmed-useful-help time, approximate blocker-to-request delay, recurrence of the same blocker, unresolved requests, and each senior’s total process minutes. Inspect aggregate results only. The mechanism is challenged if repeated questions consume similar senior time, cards frequently require correction, or searching delays help. Any senior exceeding 20 minutes is a process failure. With five newcomers, this tests feasibility and the reuse assumption, not a reliable causal effect.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Task-level stop rules and bounded escalation
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to agree in advance when continuing alone stops being useful. When a newcomer begins a task, they may privately agree with a senior on one observable escalation condition: for example, two conflicting interpretations of the protocol, a failed prerequisite check, or a decision that would invalidate subsequent work. Reaching that condition makes asking the expected next task step. This could reduce hesitation because the request follows an agreed work rule rather than requiring the newcomer to judge whether their difficulty deserves attention.

Use existing private chat to record a one-sentence condition and a safe fallback activity. Newcomers can ask before the condition occurs; the rule is permission, not an eligibility test. Participation is voluntary, and nobody must explain personal circumstances. The weekly meeting introduces the practice without reviewing individual cases.

Distribute the five newcomers across the three seniors in a rotating 2–2–1 allocation. Each senior budgets at most four minutes weekly to establish or revise conditions, fourteen minutes for private help, and two minutes for tracking and availability notices. All process work, including introduction and administration, counts toward the 20-minute limit. When capacity runs out, explicitly mark requests pending and use the agreed fallback where possible; do not silently redirect everything to one senior.

The prerequisite is work with recognizable uncertainty points and some useful fallback activity. The approach may fail for exploratory research where stopping conditions are hard to specify, or if newcomers interpret them as prohibitions against earlier questions. It changes the decision to seek help; it does not create additional expert capacity.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Compare one week of ordinary private help with two weeks using stop rules, retaining the same assignments and senior caps. Requesters optionally record approximate blocker onset, request time, first advice that enabled progress, and recurrence of the same blocker. Seniors record total process minutes; retain unresolved requests in the comparison. Inspect whether asking occurs earlier and useful help arrives sooner without increasing repeated blockers or exceeding any senior’s cap. The mechanism is challenged if conditions are usually recognized only after long delays, discourage earlier questions, or consume more setup time than they save. Five newcomers provide a feasibility check, not strong causal evidence.

DIRECT_FULL.title: Optional diagnostic request scaffold
DIRECT_FULL.proposal:
The mechanism is to reduce the expert effort needed to understand a blocker while sometimes helping the requester discover the next step themselves. Offer a short private-chat scaffold: ‘What am I trying to do? What did I expect? What happened? What single uncertainty needs an answer?’ A newcomer can attach one small relevant observation, such as an error message or conflicting instruction, with sensitive material omitted.

The scaffold is optional and takes at most three minutes. Members may send an incomplete request immediately, and ‘I do not know how to describe this’ is a valid request. Nobody must reproduce a potentially damaging action, disclose personal circumstances, or share their mistakes publicly. If writing the request reveals a solution, the newcomer can record that privately without sending the technical details.

Assign the five newcomers across three seniors in a rotating 2–2–1 pattern. Each senior has a maximum weekly budget of 20 minutes, including reading, clarification, replies, introduction, and tracking. A workable starting allocation is two minutes for administration and eighteen for requests. Seniors answer the decision or uncertainty first, using clarification only where necessary. Requests awaiting capacity remain explicitly pending. The weekly meeting only explains access and reports aggregate process observations.

This could work when substantial senior time currently goes into reconstructing context or exchanging basic clarification messages. It requires newcomers to have enough information to describe an observation and seniors to accept imperfect requests. It may add friction for unfamiliar or conceptual problems, and clearer questions will not compensate for missing expertise. No answer library or peer review is required.
DIRECT_FULL.experiment: Use one baseline week of free-form private requests followed by two weeks offering the scaffold, with unchanged routing and senior caps. Track approximate blocker-to-request delay, request-to-confirmed-useful-help time, repeated blockers, unresolved requests, and each senior’s total process minutes. Also count clarification exchanges and optionally record requests resolved during drafting. Compare all requests, including those that bypass the scaffold. The mechanism is challenged if clarification effort does not fall, drafting delays asking, or useful-help time worsens. Inspect a few voluntarily supplied, privately retained requests to see whether the scaffold actually exposes the needed decision. Results remain uncertain with this small group and changing task difficulty.

EXPAND.title: Anonymous question pooling with shared answers
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is demand aggregation: several newcomers can receive useful help from one senior answer when they share a technical uncertainty. This reduces duplicate senior work and lets members ask without attaching their identity to the question shown to seniors.

One willing newcomer acts as a rotating weekly collector through existing private chat. Members may submit a question as soon as uncertainty prevents a next step; they need not describe mistakes or personal circumstances. The collector removes identifying details, asks permission before combining or forwarding anything, and groups genuinely equivalent questions. Unique or sensitive questions remain private and can use the same senior budget individually. The collector is not expected to troubleshoot first.

Each senior has a strict weekly allowance of three minutes to inspect assigned questions, fifteen minutes to answer, and two minutes to record time and status. Assign questions by relevant expertise and remaining capacity. Each newcomer receives the answer privately and can indicate whether it enabled progress. Acknowledgements and generic advice do not count as useful help. Unanswered requests remain explicitly pending; no senior receives overflow beyond their cap.

Pooling could work when newcomers encounter common setup, method-selection, or interpretation problems. It assumes a trusted volunteer collector, some shared questions, and enough context to answer without identifying the requester. It offers confidentiality from other newcomers and potentially seniors, but the collector knows who submitted. Removing context may reduce answer quality, and distinctive research topics may remain identifiable; contributors must approve the actual forwarded wording. Collector work also needs a modest agreed limit, such as fifteen minutes weekly.

The lab meeting provides only a brief reminder that early questions are welcome and aggregate capacity information.
EXPAND.experiment: Compare one week of individual private routing with two weeks of pooling, holding each senior’s total process time at twenty minutes weekly in both conditions. Voluntarily record request-to-useful-help time, unresolved requests, recurrence of the same blocker, and all senior minutes; also record collector effort. Inspect whether pooled answers actually help multiple requesters. Reject or revise the mechanism if pooling adds waiting without reducing duplicate work, loses essential context, or exceeds either workload limit. With five newcomers, treat differences as feasibility evidence rather than a causal estimate.

EXPAND.title: Private help requests backed by reusable decision guides
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is reusable guidance: convert recurring technical blockers into short decision guides that help newcomers either progress immediately or identify precisely when to request human help. Unlike a peer relay, nobody must consult another newcomer before approaching a senior.

Begin with one or two common lab workflows that seniors already know, without soliciting accounts of individual mistakes. A guide contains a few observable checks, safe next actions, and an explicit stop condition: ‘If these checks do not resolve it, send this question privately now.’ Include situations where members should ask immediately, such as uncertainty about an irreversible experimental step. Reading or completing a guide is optional and never an eligibility requirement for help.

Distribute the guides through existing private chat. Each week, seniors divide maintenance and incoming requests within separate twenty-minute caps: up to five minutes each for guide creation or correction, thirteen minutes for private answers, and two minutes for tracking. Assign incoming requests to relevant available seniors using a simple rotating order when expertise overlaps. If demand consumes the budget, defer guide improvements and explicitly mark outstanding questions as pending. A consenting requester may suggest a generalized addition, but no conversation is copied into shared guidance without permission.

This could lower hesitation by making the boundary between independent troubleshooting and asking explicit, while amortizing senior explanations across repeated problems. It requires recurring workflows and guidance that remains accurate. It will contribute little for novel research questions and could discourage asking if presented as compulsory homework. Keep guides short, date them, and retire misleading material. The weekly meeting can normalize using the stop condition without discussing individual cases.
EXPAND.experiment: Pilot one guide for two weeks against the preceding week’s ordinary private help process, keeping the same senior time caps. Record request-to-useful-help time, unresolved requests, repeated blocker episodes, and senior minutes including authoring. Separately record voluntary reports of progress achieved through the guide, so fewer requests are not automatically interpreted as improvement. Inspect whether members recognize the stop condition and feel able to bypass the guide. Revise or stop if questions arrive later, blockers persist despite lower request counts, or maintenance costs outweigh saved explanations. The small pilot cannot establish long-term savings.

EXPAND.title: Review the next step before work stalls
EXPAND.proposal:
The mechanism is a lightweight review of intended work: newcomers can request help by sharing a proposed next step before committing substantial effort. This makes asking a routine research action and lets seniors detect missing prerequisites or unclear decisions before someone recognizes a blocker. It differs from an invitation or consultation appointment because the work artifact itself supplies the trigger and diagnostic context.

Each newcomer may privately send a three-line plan at the start of an unfamiliar task: intended outcome, proposed next action, and a decision they want checked. All fields are optional; an existing work excerpt is sufficient. Nobody must disclose mistakes, confidence levels, or personal circumstances. Reviews are optional and never become permission requirements for proceeding.

Distribute five review opportunities among the three seniors in a rotating 2–2–1 pattern, adjusted for expertise. Each senior reserves at most two minutes for routing and tracking, six minutes per initial review, and six minutes for clarification: at most twenty minutes weekly. Requests for direct help use this same allowance. The reply should confirm a justified next step, identify a concrete missing check, or explicitly state that useful guidance remains pending. Unused capacity can support another request within each senior’s cap. Overflow is acknowledged with the next available review window.

This could work when newcomers hesitate because they cannot yet formulate a question or do not know what they are missing. It assumes that short plans reveal consequential uncertainties and that seniors have enough relevant expertise. It may add little for rapidly changing tasks or blockers hidden in implementation details. Existing private chat carries plans and replies; the weekly meeting supplies only a general reminder and aggregate process observations.
EXPAND.experiment: Run a four-week pilot: two weeks of ordinary voluntary private questions with distributed senior routing, then two weeks adding next-step reviews under the same time caps. Record request-to-useful-help time, where the newcomer voluntarily confirms that a reply enabled a concrete next action; separately record pending requests and optional elapsed blocked time. Count repeat requests about the same unresolved technical issue using private, consented labels. Each senior logs all process minutes, including reading and administration. Share only lab-wide totals. The mechanism is challenged if reviews mostly produce generic approval, fail to surface actionable uncertainty earlier, increase repeated blockers, or exhaust capacity while direct requests remain pending. With five newcomers and changing tasks, this pilot can expose failure modes but cannot establish a causal improvement.
